passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — norms so fundamental to international order that no derogation from them is permissible even by treaty — occupies an uneasy position within the architecture of contemporary international law. In classical positivist theory, international legal obligations arise exclusively from the consent of sovereign states; a rule binds a state only because that state has in some fashion accepted it. Jus cogens norms, however, are said to bind all states absolutely, regardless of consent, and to invalidate any treaty provision that conflicts with them. The theoretical tension is acute: if law is a creature of consent, it is not obvious whence peremptory norms derive their authority, or why a state that never accepted a particular norm should nevertheless be bound by it.

Several responses to this difficulty have been advanced. Natural-law theorists contend that jus cogens norms derive their authority from moral principles antecedent to and independent of state practice — a position codified, at least nominally, in Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties of 1969, which defines a peremptory norm as one "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole." Yet this formulation is itself unstable: it simultaneously invokes the language of universal recognition (suggesting consent) and the language of acceptance as a community — a collective entity not obviously identical to the sum of its member states. In practice, international tribunals have identified a small cluster of recognized jus cogens norms — prohibitions on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggression — while resisting expansive claims that would bring additional norms within the peremptory category, presumably out of concern that an inflated jus cogens would corrode the consensual foundations of treaty law more broadly.

The functional consequences of jus cogens are considerable. Under the lex specialis principle, a more specific rule ordinarily prevails over a more general one in cases of conflict; but because jus cogens norms are hierarchically superior to ordinary treaty law, lex specialis cannot be invoked to displace them. Similarly, the doctrine of ultra vires — traditionally confined to the internal law of states and international organizations — acquires a new dimension when an intergovernmental body adopts a resolution that contravenes a peremptory norm: the resolution may be void ab initio, a consequence rarely invoked but theoretically available. These hierarchical implications generate a further puzzle. If a new jus cogens norm crystallizes after a treaty is concluded, Article 64 of the Vienna Convention provides that the treaty becomes void prospectively — yet determining the precise moment of crystallization, and hence the temporal boundary of the treaty's invalidity, is a task for which existing doctrine offers little guidance.

What the foregoing analysis suggests is that jus cogens, for all its theoretical ambition, functions less as a determinate legal rule than as a jurisprudential aspiration — a vocabulary through which the international legal community signals that certain values are non-negotiable, without having yet developed the adjudicative machinery necessary to give that signal consistent legal effect. Whether the International Court of Justice and other tribunals will, over time, supply the institutional architecture that the doctrine presupposes remains genuinely uncertain; what seems clear is that, in its current form, jus cogens promises more than it reliably delivers.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens is grounded in natural-law theory and has been successfully codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although jus cogens norms are theoretically capable of invalidating treaty provisions, international tribunals have consistently refused to apply them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jus cogens represents an ambitious but theoretically unsettled doctrine whose functional consequences remain significant yet whose adjudicative implementation remains inadequate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The principal defect of jus cogens is that the doctrine relies on the concept of consent while simultaneously denying that consent is necessary for legal obligation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: International law would be better served if the International Court of Justice formally enumerated a comprehensive list of peremptory norms.

explanations.correct: The passage traces jus cogens across its theoretical tensions (paragraphs 1–2), functional consequences (paragraph 3), and ultimate shortfall between aspiration and reliable legal effect (paragraph 4). C integrates all four paragraphs without overstating or narrowing.
explanations.A: Too narrow and inaccurate — the passage treats the natural-law grounding as contested and the Vienna Convention formulation as 'unstable,' not as a successful codification.
explanations.B: Overstates one tendency — tribunals have identified some norms; 'consistently refused to apply' misreads the passage's nuanced description.
explanations.D: Captures only the tension described in paragraphs 1–2, omitting the functional and institutional dimensions of paragraphs 3–4; also slightly mischaracterizes the argument.
explanations.E: The passage implies uncertainty about whether tribunals will develop doctrine, but never recommends a formal enumeration — this conflates a descriptive gap with a prescriptive proposal the author does not make.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward jus cogens as it currently functions in international law can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified admiration for the moral vision the doctrine embodies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism about whether the doctrine's theoretical ambitions are matched by its practical legal effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: firm conviction that jus cogens will eventually be abandoned in favor of purely consent-based treaty obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: hostility toward the international tribunals that have declined to expand the recognized set of peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifference to the theoretical foundations of international law so long as practical outcomes are consistent.

explanations.correct: The closing paragraph explicitly characterizes jus cogens as 'a jurisprudential aspiration' that 'promises more than it reliably delivers,' and calls its institutional future 'genuinely uncertain' — language of measured skepticism, not hostility or admiration.
explanations.A: The author acknowledges the doctrine's ambition but does not express admiration; the closing assessment is critical, not laudatory.
explanations.C: The author does not predict abandonment; the question of whether tribunals will supply necessary architecture is described as 'genuinely uncertain,' not as foreclosed.
explanations.D: The author characterizes the tribunals' restraint as 'presumably' motivated by concern for consensual treaty foundations — a sympathetic explanation, not hostile criticism.
explanations.E: The passage devotes considerable attention to theoretical foundations; indifference to theory is the opposite of the author's orientation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; the theoretical problem it poses for an established framework is articulated; responses to that problem are examined; functional consequences of the doctrine are analyzed; and the author assesses the doctrine's current state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and endorsed; competing theories about its origin are contrasted; the doctrine's historical development is traced chronologically; and a proposal for institutional reform is advanced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A theoretical tension is identified; two conflicting judicial interpretations of that tension are presented; a third interpretation is offered and rejected; and the passage concludes by siding with the first interpretation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A distinction between two branches of international law is drawn; each branch is illustrated with a case study; inconsistencies between the case studies are noted; and a recommendation for legislative reform is offered.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A foundational principle of international law is shown to be internally contradictory; a historical account of its origins is provided; and the author argues that the principle should be abolished.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines jus cogens and its tension with positivism; paragraph 2 examines responses (natural-law theory, Vienna Convention language, tribunal practice); paragraph 3 analyzes functional consequences (lex specialis, ultra vires, crystallization problem); paragraph 4 delivers the author's overall assessment. A tracks this four-step structure accurately.
explanations.B: The author does not endorse jus cogens, and the passage does not trace historical development chronologically or propose institutional reform.
explanations.C: The passage does not present two conflicting judicial interpretations and then offer a third to be rejected; that structure is fabricated.
explanations.D: No case studies in the conventional sense are presented, and no legislative recommendation is made.
explanations.E: The author does not argue the principle should be abolished — only that it currently 'promises more than it reliably delivers.'

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties defines a peremptory norm as one

choices.label: A
choices.text: that has been explicitly consented to by every member state of the international community.

choices.label: B
choices.text: from which no derogation is permissible under any circumstances, including in times of armed conflict.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole."

choices.label: D
choices.text: that has been formally identified as such by the International Court of Justice in a binding opinion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: whose content is derived from moral principles antecedent to and independent of state practice.

explanations.correct: The passage quotes Article 53 verbatim in paragraph 2: a peremptory norm is one 'accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole.' C reproduces this directly.
explanations.A: The passage notes that the Vienna Convention language simultaneously invokes universal recognition and community acceptance — it does not require explicit consent by every member state, and the author treats this as an ambiguity rather than a clear requirement.
explanations.B: This paraphrases the general concept of jus cogens from paragraph 1 (no derogation permitted), not the Vienna Convention's definitional language asked about.
explanations.D: The passage does not attribute identification authority exclusively to the ICJ; this is an unsupported addition.
explanations.E: This describes the natural-law theorists' position, not the Vienna Convention's definitional language.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that international tribunals have been reluctant to expand the list of recognized jus cogens norms primarily because

choices.label: A
choices.text: they lack jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes involving claims that a treaty violates a peremptory norm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the natural-law basis of jus cogens has been formally rejected by the states that comprise the international community.

choices.label: C
choices.text: an expanded roster of peremptory norms could undermine the consensual foundations upon which ordinary treaty law rests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: no procedural mechanism exists by which a tribunal may declare a norm peremptory without legislative authorization.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the prohibitions already recognized — on genocide, slavery, torture, and aggression — are widely regarded as exhausting the category.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that tribunals resist expansive jus cogens claims 'presumably out of concern that an inflated jus cogens would corrode the consensual foundations of treaty law more broadly.' C paraphrases this inference directly.
explanations.A: The passage does not suggest jurisdictional barriers; the restraint is described as a policy concern, not a jurisdictional one.
explanations.B: The passage does not say natural-law theory has been formally rejected; it says the Vienna Convention formulation is 'unstable,' a more nuanced claim.
explanations.D: No procedural mechanism gap is mentioned; the passage's explanation is substantive, not procedural.
explanations.E: The passage identifies those four norms as examples of what has been recognized, not as an exhaustive category that tribunals treat as closed by consensus.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the lex specialis principle in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how jus cogens creates a hierarchical exception to an otherwise general rule of treaty interpretation, thereby showing the doctrine's functional significance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce the concept of ultra vires as a mechanism for invalidating resolutions adopted by intergovernmental bodies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why the Vienna Convention's definition of peremptory norms is theoretically unstable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that classical positivism is incompatible with any form of hierarchical legal ordering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that lex specialis should be reformed to accommodate the hierarchical demands of jus cogens norms.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph opens by noting that lex specialis ordinarily governs conflicts between more specific and more general rules, then immediately explains that jus cogens overrides this default because of its hierarchical superiority. The function is to illustrate a concrete functional consequence of jus cogens — showing the doctrine actually alters legal outcomes in practice.
explanations.B: Ultra vires is introduced separately after lex specialis; the lex specialis discussion does not function to introduce ultra vires.
explanations.C: The Vienna Convention's instability is discussed in paragraph 2, not paragraph 3; lex specialis plays no role in that analysis.
explanations.D: Classical positivism is the concern of paragraph 1; the third paragraph does not return to refute positivism but rather analyzes functional consequences.
explanations.E: The author makes no reform proposal regarding lex specialis; the discussion is descriptive and analytical.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's conclusion in the final paragraph that jus cogens "promises more than it reliably delivers"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states have recently argued in treaty negotiations that certain environmental protection obligations should be elevated to the status of jus cogens norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The International Court of Justice, in a series of judgments issued over the past two decades, has consistently and successfully voided treaty provisions found to conflict with recognized jus cogens norms, producing durable changes in state behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal scholars continue to disagree about whether the natural-law or the consent-based account of jus cogens better explains the doctrine's authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Article 64 of the Vienna Convention has never been invoked in an actual case before an international tribunal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some states have incorporated jus cogens norms into their domestic constitutions, creating parallel enforcement mechanisms at the national level.

explanations.correct: The author's conclusion is that jus cogens lacks the 'adjudicative machinery necessary to give that signal consistent legal effect.' If the ICJ has in fact been consistently applying jus cogens to void treaty provisions, and that application has durably altered state behavior, then the doctrine is delivering on its promises — directly undermining the author's claim.
explanations.A: States advocating expansion of jus cogens in negotiations supports the doctrine's aspirational status but says nothing about effective adjudicative implementation; it is consistent with, not contrary to, the author's conclusion.
explanations.C: Ongoing scholarly disagreement about jus cogens's theoretical foundation actually reinforces the author's picture of theoretical instability, rather than undermining it.
explanations.D: That Article 64 has never been invoked supports the author's claim that the doctrine's hierarchical implications are 'rarely invoked' — this strengthens rather than weakens the conclusion.
explanations.E: Domestic constitutional incorporation is a parallel mechanism, but the author's claim concerns international adjudicative machinery; domestic incorporation does not directly address whether the international doctrine reliably delivers.
